# Empowering Tomorrow: Exploring AI Two-Sided Model Research


Explore InterDigital’s research into AI two-sided models and how independently trained AI systems could interoperate to advance wireless and video technologies.


October 2026


InterDigital Comms


[AI](https://www.interdigital.com/blog?tags=AI)


InterDigital’s wireless, video, and AI research is anchored by a common goal to enable devices, systems, and technologies to work together to empower deeper digital connections and experiences. Driven by the principles of interoperability, we are exploring the foundations of a common "language" that could allow AI models developed independently and deployed across different entities to work together seamlessly.


InterDigital’s Marketing and Communications team sat down with Akshay Malhotra, Senior Staff Machine Learning Researcher in the AI Lab, to discuss the team’s early research on AI two-sided models and an application of this work to AI-based compression of channel state information (CSI) data. This work explores an important frontier where “standardized” AI interfaces do not exist, and pioneers research that is preparing for a world where pervasive AI models depend on interoperability to be most effective.


* *This interview has been edited and condensed for editorial purposes.*


**InterDigital: Akshay, your work is exploring a truly novel and complex area of AI. How might you explain your research to a high schooler?**


**Akshay** : Data compression of any form is a very important problem. On a daily basis, to share and transmit information, you must compress it because the complete data is too large to send. This is true for any form of data – images, videos, or even wireless information. Think about taking a photo with your phone. The image contains a lot of information, so your phone compresses it to make the file easier to store or send. When you open the photo, software decodes that compressed information and reconstructs the image for you to view.


With how technology is progressing lately, we’re talking more and more about deep-learning-based compression and decompression frameworks. These frameworks work by training the encoder, or compressor, and the decoder, or decompressor, together. Both of these components are trained jointly end-to-end.


If you train these task and domain specific encoder and decoder components of a model separately, for settings like compression or decompression, then they will not be able to talk to each other. In other words, they would have different interpretations of the information that is carried and shared between them. They have not agreed on a common interpretation, or common language, to describe this information.


So, a key question becomes: “How can you train two models independently but make sure that they easily interoperate with each other?” And “what needs to be defined to do that?” Our research, strongly influenced by specific challenges our colleagues have encountered in data exchange and compression in wireless networks, explores whether these two operations can be *learned* without any online collaboration, and what is the minimal amount of information that needs to be defined, exchanged, or agreed upon to ensure these two models can interoperate.


**InterDigital: How are you tackling this new problem that you’ve identified?**


**Akshay** : The language analogy is useful here. When two people share a common language, they can communicate even if they learned it separately. If they do not speak the same language, they need either a translator or a small set of agreed upon rules that helps them understand one another.


We are taking a similar approach with AI models. Rather than requiring two models to develop exactly the same internal language, we give them the same basic "rules" during training.


Normally, independently trained models can organize the same information in very different ways. We add a training rule that encourages each model to preserve the same underlying structure or "shape" in its internal representation. Their representations may not be identical, but important pieces of information remain connected in similar ways.


Each model follows the rule independently, using the input data or a transformation of it as its reference. The models do not need to see each other, exchange parameters, or reveal their architectures during training.


**InterDigital: In essence, your research is trying to identify the minimum amount of baseline information needed to reach that “third language,” or compatible representation?**


**Akshay** : Yes, or at least that’s the goal. We want to figure out what is the minimum amount of information the models need to share, or develop a training strategy that requires minimal coordination, so that independently trained models converge to this common language or compatible latent space. Our research has been conducted with a limited scope to examine baseline compatible representations for channel state information compression in wireless networks.


**InterDigital: Why is greater interoperability between different AI models so important?**


**Akshay:** I feel that interoperability across models is important as AI makes inroads in the fields of wireless communications and video compression. Right now, the deployment and standardization of AI in these fields is in its early stages. Especially on the wireless side, we are beginning to see active discussions around exactly what role AI will play, though we’re still **some way** from AI being meaningfully deployed. Hopefully, from 6G onwards, we will start seeing more AI-enabled approaches being standardized and deployed.


These issues will become more prominent when models have to be deployed across distinct entities that must interoperate and work with each other. If a model is only deployed on a single entity and does everything end-to-end, then there is no interoperability issue.


The problem is when two models, or two pieces of a model, are deployed at distinct points and are separated by a barrier because those devices might be owned by different companies. That’s where these interoperability issues become more prevalent.


We expect to see it happen as AI progresses. We expect there will be a need for more and more AI models to interact with each other out-of-the-box after deployment. Hopefully, our research will be important moving forward to enable such settings.


**InterDigital: Who is the ultimate beneficiary of this innovation?**


**Akshay** : That’s a very valid question, I would think it could be anybody. But more realistically, probably device makers or people who are supporting some kind of application. This is a very generalized framework, so it could potentially be applied across several domains.


Consider an AI-based data-compression system. A device maker may want to create an encoder optimized for its own hardware, while another company may want to create a decoder optimized for its platform. Each company may have proprietary model designs that it does not want to disclose.


Today, those companies might need to coordinate closely, share large amounts of training data, or agree to use models developed by one party. An interoperable approach could give each company more control over its own component while still allowing other components to work together. That flexibility could make systems easier to improve, replace, and adapt over time.


**InterDigital: Is the intention to standardize a framework for AI models?**


**Akshay** : It’s about giving people more flexibility, while ensuring things still work with each other.


You can design your model and neural network however you want and train them however you want; all we’re going to do is specify a few different things. For example, a framework could specify a small addition to the training objective that encourages each model to preserve the same underlying structure. It could also define a limited amount of information to be shared afterward, such as a small set of examples and the representations each model produces.


We are exploring what the minimum requirements should be, such that they allow you to keep your proprietary information to yourself, but still allow your models to work with any other model, operator, or company’s design out-of-the-box.


You don’t need to standardize all of the language in the middle. All you need to standardize are these small pieces and a couple of small changes to your training strategy. If people ensure that they do that, their models will interoperate with each other. We’re trying to figure out what are those pieces that need to be defined or standardized to allow this to happen.


**InterDigital: Did our expertise in wireless and video influence this research at all?**


**Akshay:** Yes. We initially started thinking about this problem because, in both video and wireless, we were seeing AI enablement becoming increasingly distributed. Different parts of an AI pipeline may run on different devices or be developed by different entities. These components need a way to exchange information and work together.


For example, in the video community, MPEG has been working on Feature Coding for Machines (FCM), where an AI model can be split across different systems and the intermediate features produced by one part of the model are compressed and transmitted to another. This creates an interesting interface between the models on the two sides.


Once you have such an interface, multiple practical questions arise: Who trains the models on either side? Does one entity design both components and ask the other to adopt them as is? Can each entity create its own model component? And how much data, model information, or intellectual property do they need to exchange to make those independently-developed components work together?


We saw a very similar question in wireless. You may have a device manufacturer on one side and a network vendor on the other. They are different entities, but their systems still need to be compatible. If an AI encoder runs on the device and an AI decoder runs in the network, both sides need a way to interpret the information being exchanged.


One possible approach is for an entity or company to use its model to process a very large reference dataset and share all the resulting representations so that another organization can train a compatible model. In this scenario, the companies don’t need to exchange their models. They don’t have to say how their models are being trained, but they still work with each other.


Still, the amount of information exchange this requires can be very large. The question, then, is how do we enable these things realistically with a limited amount of information exchange, while standardizing the small pieces that will enable such a framework to happen across any domain?


**InterDigital: This is really fascinating. While this research is at an early and theoretical stage, looking ahead, what could this potentially enable?**


**Akshay** : One direction we’re looking to explore is related to vision-language models. These systems typically include a vision encoder that converts an image into tokens that a language model can interpret. Today, these components are generally developed and trained closely together so that they share a compatible internal language or representation.


What we want to determine next is whether you can develop and train the vision and the language components separately, and still make them interoperate. For example, could a vision encoder developed by one company interoperate with a language model developed by another, without retraining the entire system?


This could enable a multi-vendor ecosystem that allows users to select and combine specific components based on their needs. Such a framework could also support distributed deployment in resource-constrained environments, with different components running on a device, at the network edge, or in the cloud.


Ultimately, we want to understand whether a lightweight interoperability framework could allow independently developed AI components to work together.


**InterDigital: What are the next steps for this research?**


**Akshay** : So far, this is a very conceptual idea with very limited existing research on it. A few papers over the last couple of years have touched on this problem, but the solutions are fairly basic and not well grounded.


I believe our work positions us at the forefront of this research, advancing interoperability between AI models. Our AI team has developed several possible approaches and has begun testing them across different tasks and datasets.


Our recent and ongoing research* examines whether training models to preserve the underlying structure of the data can help them develop compatible internal representations without requiring direct coordination during training. We are also exploring whether the same principles can be extended to larger systems.


We will also demonstrate a practical application of this research at the 2026 Brooklyn 6G Summit. The demo applies our interoperability approach to AI-based compression of channel state information (CSI) data. Running live on an[OAI](https://openairinterface.org/) (Open Air Interface) based wireless testbed, it will show that encoder and decoder models trained independently using our approach can work together and achieve performance close to that of models trained jointly, end-to-end.


** Editor’s Note: Akshay and members of the AI Lab recently published a paper exploring the potential for AI two-sided models. Learn more below.*


**Topology-Preserving Regularization for Interoperable Representations**


As large, powerful pre-trained models become more prevalent, there is growing interest in developing methods that allow different neural networks to be seamlessly combined with little or no direct communication between them. Take autoencoder-based data compression as an example: the ability to independently choose architectures and train encoder and decoder models, while still ensuring they work together, could fundamentally transform how such models are built, deployed, and updated. In this work, our engineers introduce a novel approach that leverages topological regularization to align the latent spaces of two independently trained autoencoder models, entirely eliminating the need for coordination during training. Our engineers provide a conditional theoretical analysis showing how the structural agreement encouraged by our regularizer can translate into approximate geometric compatibility between independently learned representations. Reconstruction experiments validate this approach empirically, substantially narrowing the interoperability gap across multiple datasets.


Read the full paper[here](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19401) .
